title: Essentialism
author: Greg McKeown
theme: Doing fewer things, chosen deliberately and done well, produces a far greater contribution than spreading effort across everything that asks for attention.
summary: Greg McKeown argues that many capable people feel busy yet stretched thin, making small progress in a dozen directions instead of real progress in one. His remedy is essentialism: the disciplined pursuit of fewer, better things. It is not a time-management trick but a way of deciding where to put your energy so that your highest contribution gets the attention it deserves.

He begins with a warning he calls the paradox of success. Clear focus brings results, results bring new opportunities and requests, and saying yes to all of them scatters the very focus that produced the success in the first place.

The essentialist mindset rests on three beliefs. First, we always have a choice about how to spend our time, even when it does not feel that way. Second, very few activities are truly vital, while most are of minor value. Third, trade-offs are unavoidable, so the real question is not how to do everything but which problem we want to have.

The book then follows a three-step process. To explore, essentialists make space to think, notice what really matters as a good reporter looks for the heart of a story, protect sleep and play, and apply strict selection: if an option is not an obvious yes, treat it as a no.

To eliminate, they set a clear purpose that makes later decisions easier, learn to decline requests politely but firmly, abandon commitments that no longer pay off despite past investment, edit away the unnecessary, and set boundaries.

To execute, they build buffers for the unexpected, remove the main obstacle slowing progress, celebrate small wins, design routines that make the right action automatic, and stay attentive to what matters right now.
McKeown's closing point is that a life designed around the essential is both more effective and more satisfying, because it puts us in charge of our own choices.
takeaway: Treat every commitment as a trade-off: discern the vital few, decline the rest gracefully, and make execution of what remains as effortless as possible.

options: Doing more tasks in less time
The disciplined pursuit of fewer, better things
Delegating all routine work
Living with as few possessions as possible
questions.why: The book frames essentialism as deliberately choosing less so that what remains gets done well.

questions.q: What is the 'paradox of success' described in the book?
options: Successful people rarely enjoy their success
Success always depends on luck
Success brings new options that scatter the focus which created it
Success is easier for teams than for individuals
questions.why: Focus yields results, results attract more demands, and accepting them all undermines the original focus.

questions.q: Which belief is part of the essentialist mindset?
options: Trade-offs are unavoidable, so we must choose which ones to make
Every opportunity is equally valuable
Busyness is a sign of importance
Choice is mostly an illusion at work
questions.why: Essentialists accept that they cannot have it all and decide deliberately what to give up.

questions.q: What are the three stages of the essentialist process?
options: Plan, do, check
Listen, learn, lead
Prioritise, delegate, review
Explore, eliminate, execute
questions.why: The book is organised around exploring options, eliminating the nonessential, and executing what remains.

questions.q: What selection rule does McKeown suggest when evaluating an option?
options: Accept anything that could possibly help
If it is not a clear yes, treat it as a no
Choose whatever is most urgent
Follow the majority opinion
questions.why: Applying strict criteria prevents mildly attractive options from crowding out the truly important ones.

questions.q: Why does the book treat sleep and play as essential rather than optional?
options: They are required by most employers
They are rewards to be earned after work is done
They protect and renew our ability to think clearly and make good choices
They fill time that would otherwise be wasted
questions.why: Rest and play sustain the clarity and creativity needed to discern what matters.

questions.q: What does McKeown advise about commitments that no longer add value but have absorbed much past effort?
options: Keep going so the past investment is not wasted
Hand them to a colleague
Wait until they fail on their own
Let them go despite what has already been invested
questions.why: Holding on because of sunk costs keeps us trapped in nonessential work.

questions.q: What is the purpose of declining requests gracefully?
options: To protect the essential while preserving respect and relationships
To avoid all extra responsibility
To appear more important than others
To keep options open for later
questions.why: A clear, polite no guards one's priorities without damaging trust.

questions.q: In the execution stage, why build buffers into plans?
options: To slow the team down
To prepare for the unexpected so plans do not collapse
To justify larger budgets
To avoid setting deadlines
questions.why: Allowing extra time and resources for surprises keeps essential work on track.

questions.q: Which practice does the book recommend to make essential work feel effortless over time?
options: Waiting for motivation to strike
Taking on more projects at once
Designing routines that make the right action automatic
Rewriting goals every week
questions.why: Routines remove repeated decisions, so important work happens with little friction.
